newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin wants shift EU to jobs, growth.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin wants shift EU to jobs, growth.

text.p: Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, scenting an upset victory in France's looming parliamentary election, said on Friday he would seek to re-orient the European Union towards jobs and growth.

"Is victory possible? I believe it is, but nothing is decided," the 59-year-old Jospin, buoyed by opinion polls showing the left in striking range of victory in the May 25-June 1 vote, told RMC radio.
"The trend is in our favour, we are on an upwards trend," he said after a poll showed the ruling centre-right's lead narrowing to a one-seat majority in the National Assembly.
Jospin also said in a newspaper article published on Friday, in response to a column by President Jacques Chirac, that one pillar of Socialist policy would be "respect for Europe".
The Socialists wanted a single European currency but it would have to be under specific conditions, he said.
"We want Europe without undoing France. We do not want Europe to dissolve into globalisation," Jospin said,

"We want to re-orient European policy towards growth and jobs," he said, urging faith in a "world which does not have to be this jungle we are promised by the self-interested fatalists of unrestricted liberalism and finance".
Jospin's article followed Chirac's column earlier this week urging French voters to re-elect the centre-right.
The left-wing daily Liberation, calling the confrontation a draw, said "a botched counter-offensive responds to a botched attack".

Prime Minister Alain Juppe told an election rally that Jospin had failed to say how he would implement his job-creating platform without raising taxes and solve differences with his Communist allies who are calling for a referendum on the single currency.
Jospin told RMC radio he would finance his programme by redistributing existing taxes without raising them.
Pledging policies based on respect for Europe, democracy and the individual, he said France needed to restore confidence after a string of broken promises and errors by right and left.
"It will only do so by finding confidence in its leaders. It's a question of respect...the foundation of this future we want to build," the white-haired ex-education minister wrote.
Voters, weary of political sleaze and rising unemployment, dumped the Socialists in the last National Assembly elections in 1993. Both factors now threaten Juppe's centre-right coalition.
"We have to know how to draw the lessons of the 10 years during which we were in government. I take responsibility, and the Socialist party with me, for the past errors," Jospin said.
Polls show many voters are disillusioned with politicians and believe neither the Socialists nor Juppe's coalition have answers to their main concern -- record unemployment of 12.8 percent.
Jospin, who has a reputation of being short on charisma but long on honesty, lost to Chirac in the 1995 presidential poll.
He described Chirac's criticisms of the left's platform and record as "negative, partisan and unfair" but otherwise steered clear of personal barbs.
An Ipsos survey for the weekly Le Point projected that the ruling coalition would win 290 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, just one more than would be needed for a majority.
It said the Socialists and their allies would get 264 seats, the Communists 22 and the far-right National Front one.
It was the narrowest lead for Juppe's coalition since Chirac, elected to a seven-year term ending in 2002, gambled his presidency by calling the early election.

Chirac called the vote saying that the government needed a new impetus to combat unemployment and enter a single European currency from a position of strength. But he risks becoming a lame duck for the next five years if the left wins.
